tracks.title: The network is a service, not a permission
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 10 — networking. A deep-dive, under the nexus. Here's the idea the whole page turns on. A workbook never opens a socket… in either direction. It hands the engine a destination and some bytes… and the engine — which holds the connections, the TLS stack, and the credentials — decides, connects, audits, and answers. [curious] That one inversion buys things a firewall can't. HTTPS without shipping any crypto. Signed API calls without ever holding the key. A network you can revoke mid-flight. And — the part nobody else does — standard tools that think they have sockets… while every single connect is checked.

tracks.title: The boolean lie
tracks.text: First — the boolean lie. Every sandbox vendor says the same three words. No network by default. [sarcastic] Read the code, and it's usually one boolean. Off… and the sandbox is useless — your workbook can't call an API, can't reach a database, can't fetch a thing. On… and it inherits the whole host network. The cloud metadata endpoint that hands out credentials. Localhost, where your control plane listens. Every box on your LAN. There is no third setting — so people ship the dangerous one, and hope the prompt-injected agent never asks for the metadata address. [sighs] That's the hole this engine was built to close. And the question it answers is the one a boolean never can. What exactly can a workbook reach… who decided… and where's the log?

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. In a workbook, networking is a brokered service — not a permission. The guest never opens a socket in either direction. It hands the engine a destination and bytes… and the engine connects, checks every resolved address, audits the attempt, and returns the answer. And it's granted by derivation from a capability profile — never by default. Default is no network. Not as a setting you could forget to flip — a workbook on the minimal or compute profile gets no HTTP linked in, no socket pool, no DNS at all. Only a profile that grants net… or browse… derives any host network. The network is something the engine renders for the guest — the way a kitchen renders a meal you never cooked.

tracks.title: The two egress lanes
tracks.text: Now — the two egress lanes. There are exactly two paths a guest can take outbound, and both are mediated. The first is the standard lane — the WASI HTTP and sockets seam that unmodified tools already speak. A program written for any WebAssembly host, calling plain fetch… lands here and gets safe brokered network without knowing it. The second is the dock lane — explicit host imports a guest written for Workbooks calls on purpose. Host HTTP get… host TCP… host UDP… host TLS. [curious] And here's a subtlety worth holding onto. The two lanes gate differently. The Rust dock gates by presence — a non-network profile simply doesn't get the import merged in. The function isn't there to call. The JavaScript dock gates by behavior — it always imports everything, but a denied capability returns minus one, which shows up to JavaScript as a null. Two styles… one rule underneath. So picture the whole thing as one funnel with two mouths. A request enters from either lane — standard or dock — and they immediately merge onto the same four checks. First, the SSRF floor — deny the internal targets. Second, the allow-list — the per-instance scope. Third, the rate floor. And fourth, the audit. Only what survives all four reaches the public internet. There is no path that skips the cadence… because the guest never holds the socket that would let it.

tracks.title: The SSRF floor
tracks.text: The SSRF floor. This is the part that's always on — under both lanes, before you scope anything. It's a deny set of address families a guest has no business reaching, and it's the same list in two implementations — one in Elixir, one in Rust — so neither lane is a hole in the other. Loopback. The private ranges. Link-local — which is where the cloud metadata address lives. Carrier-grade NAT. Multicast, broadcast, and all the IPv6 equivalents. Plus the two tricks attackers reach for — an IPv4 address mapped into IPv6, re-checked as the v4 address it really is… and NAT64-style addresses with an internal v4 smuggled inside, re-classified before the verdict. And if a name won't resolve — the answer is deny. Not, try anyway. [excited] And this isn't a spec we hope holds. A red-team test fires a real browser-grade guest at ten obfuscated internal targets, calling standard fetch, and every one must come back blocked. Picture the probe list read aloud. A request to the metadata address… blocked. To loopback… blocked. To a ten-dot private address… blocked. To a one-ninety-two-dot-one-sixty-eight LAN address… blocked. To carrier-grade NAT… blocked. To IPv6 loopback… blocked. To the v4-mapped-v6 smuggle… blocked. Even the trick of putting a username and password in front of loopback to fool the parser… blocked. And then — a request to example dot com, a plain public host… two hundred, OK. So the verdict, in one sentence. The floor's whole job is to stop a guest from reaching inward — at your infrastructure, your metadata, your LAN. It does not, by itself, stop a guest from talking to an arbitrary public host. That's a different concern, with a different tool, and it's opt-in — coming up in a moment.

tracks.title: Resolve-then-pin
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — skippable — resolve, then pin. A deny list on IPs has a famous hole. DNS rebinding. The attacker's hostname resolves to a public address when you check it… then to loopback a millisecond later, when your HTTP client re-resolves it to actually connect. The fix is to resolve once… and pin. Resolve the hostname a single time, check every address that came back against the floor, and then connect to the pinned address — never to the hostname, which a naive client would just look up again. So walk it as a story. The guest asks for a hostname. The engine resolves it exactly once, and freezes the answer. It judges every address that came back — and if any one is internal, the story ends right there. Otherwise it dials the frozen address… but keeps the original name on the TLS handshake, so virtual hosts and certificate checks still work. And a redirect doesn't reset the rules — it's just hop two, checked like hop one, up to five hops. A public URL that bounces you to an internal one… gets caught on the second check. The hostname the guest typed never gets a second, exploitable resolution.

tracks.title: TCP, UDP, TLS without a socket
tracks.text: TCP, UDP, and TLS — without a socket. The dock lane's headline is three one-shot brokers. Each takes a destination and bytes, does the whole request and response on the host, and hands back the answer — the guest never sees a file descriptor. Picture the three of them as a little table, and I'll give you the verdict on each. First, the TCP broker — a one-megabyte cap, a ten-second timeout — covers plain HTTP, Redis, and line protocols. Second, the UDP broker — a sixty-five-kilobyte cap, a five-second timeout — for DNS, NTP, and STUN. Third, the TLS broker — one megabyte, ten seconds — and this is the standout. Two of those rows hide something better than a protocol. The UDP broker connects its socket to the pinned peer, so the kernel itself drops any datagram from a different source — and then checks the source again anyway. Belt and suspenders, against reply-spoofing. And the TLS broker… [excited] the host does the handshake — verify-peer against the system roots, the hostname pinned on the SNI — the guest sends plaintext and gets decrypted bytes back. A guest that contains no crypto at all… gets HTTPS. Picture the guest code. It declares one external function — host TLS, taking a host, a port, a request buffer, and an output buffer. It sends a plain GET request line. The host does everything secure, and hands back the decrypted reply. Return minus one means denied — one error code, and you check the audit ring for the reason why. The JavaScript twin lands on the same import — get a URL, and a null means denied. And here's the payoff. An unmodified fetch, in bundled npm JavaScript, is backed by that exact same seam. Node-style code doesn't open a socket — it asks the engine, and it doesn't know the difference. One last import earns a mention, because it does something the guest can't do alone. Host HTTP get many takes a batch of URLs — capped at sixty-four, a deliberate floor against amplification — and the runtime fetches them concurrently, sixteen at a time. A single-threaded guest gets real parallel fan-out… it could never produce on its own.

tracks.title: Allow-lists and the DNS-off trick
tracks.text: Another depth rung — allow-lists, and the DNS-off trick. The floor blocks internal targets. To bound a guest to a specific set of public ones, an instance can carry an allow-list — host names, host and port, wildcard suffixes — and the moment that list is non-empty, it's default-deny. Only what's listed gets through. And crucially, this sits on top of the floor, not instead of it. Scope a guest to one-dot-one-dot-one-dot-one… and eight-dot-eight-dot-eight-dot-eight — a perfectly public DNS server — is still denied, because it isn't on the list. Now the sharp trick. What happens when the list is all raw IP addresses. A guest that can resolve hostnames can leak data by encoding it into DNS queries to an attacker's subdomain — the lookup itself is the leak, even if no connection completes. So when the list is all IPs, the engine turns off name lookup entirely. An IP-scoped guest cannot resolve names at all — which means it cannot leak through DNS. And the test proves it bluntly. Scoped to one address… picture three connection attempts. First, to that one listed address — OK. Second, to a different public address, not on the list — error, default-deny. Third, to a hostname — error, because there is no DNS at all. One honest note on maturity. Today that allow-list is set programmatically, per instance — it's a real, enforced option, exercised in the tests — but there is no author-facing syntax for it yet. No line you write at the top of a workbook. The enforcement is solid… the declaration surface is still to come. And we won't pretend otherwise.

tracks.title: The engine holds the credentials
tracks.text: The engine holds the credentials. The nexus lesson promises that secrets stay in the engine — this is the mechanism. There are four flavors of the same move… the guest acts, the engine authenticates… and none of them ever shows the workbook a secret. First — browse-fetch. A typed import where the component sees only a JSON string back. The guest asks for a page… the engine fetches it. Second — LLM complete. The host holds the model API key. The workbook calls a model, and never sees the key that paid for the call. Third — and this is the sharpest — the secret broker. There is no read operation. The only thing a guest can do with a secret… is sign. An HMAC with the tenant's named key. The guest gets a signature back, and authenticates a webhook or an API call without ever possessing the credential. [curious] You can't leak what you were never handed. And fourth — data-source plugins. A manifest names the URL and the environment keys, the token is resolved on the host, and the egress runs on the host's client. The plugin never holds the raw key… and never opens a socket itself. It's the inversion again — applied to authentication. A normal program proves who it is by holding a secret. A workbook proves who it is… by asking the engine to prove it.

tracks.title: The server flip
tracks.text: The server flip. Everything so far was outbound. Serving flips it — and the inversion holds. The host owns the listening socket. The guest never accepts a connection. Per request, the engine hands the guest the bytes, and takes back the response — and the rate check fires before the guest runs, so a flood costs zero guest CPU. So picture the path of one request. A client sends an HTTP request. It hits the host listener, which rate-checks it first — answering with a four-twenty-nine if it's a flood — before any guest code runs at all. Then the host hands the guest the request, shaped as plain bytes — method, path, headers, a blank line, body. The guest handles it, and returns bytes. The host wraps them and answers the client. And the standard seam carries the same discipline as the rest of the engine — a fresh instance per request for isolation, mid-flight revocation that answers five-oh-three, a per-client rate limit that answers four-twenty-nine, a four-megabyte body cap that answers four-thirteen, and a streaming mode with a deadline trap against compute abuse. [excited] But here's the line that matters most. Any outbound the serving guest makes, mid-request, is still brokered through the SSRF floor. A served app cannot be turned into a pivot into your network — and the test asserts exactly that. The served body reads… outbound, blocked.

tracks.title: Revoke, rate, audit
tracks.text: Last depth rung — revoke, rate, audit — what the operator actually sees. Three controls wrap every broker call. First — revocation. An in-memory set, checked on each call. Revoke a tenant, and the next broker call fails — mid-flight, with no teardown of the running guest. Second — rate limiting. A generous floor, about two thousand broker calls per second per tenant, tuned to catch a runaway… not to meter usage. Third — audit, the memory. Every denial bumps a counter keyed by broker, outcome, and reason… lands in a hundred-and-twenty-eight-entry forensics ring… and fires a telemetry event you can route to Prometheus or a SIEM. And the targets in that ring are truncated to five-hundred-and-twelve bytes — because the strings are guest-controlled, and an un-capped string is a memory-exhaustion vector all by itself. Picture the operator at the console. They ask for the stats… and get back a map — net allowed, four hundred and twelve. Net denied for SSRF, three. TCP denied for SSRF, one. They ask for the recent denials… and get the last attempts, each with its target and a timestamp — there's the metadata address, caught in the act. And they revoke a tenant by name… and the very next call from that tenant comes back, error, revoked. The numbers that anchor it all are worth saying out loud — about two thousand broker calls a second per tenant; fifty thousand connect attempts per ten seconds per instance, counted even when denied, so a guest that hammers the floor still hits the ceiling; sixty-four URLs per batch. What did it try, and where's the log… has a literal answer.

tracks.title: What it isn't
tracks.text: The honest part — what it isn't. The model is strong because it's narrow… and the narrowness has edges worth naming. First — one-shot, not persistent. The brokers are request and response. There's no long-lived connection a guest holds — no WebSocket client kept open across many beats. Streaming inbound exists, for serving. Persistent outbound from a guest does not. Second — allow-lists aren't author-declarable yet. They're enforced per instance, but there's no syntax to write the scope at the top of a workbook today. Third — the floor stops inward, not outward. It blocks internal targets — metadata, LAN, loopback. It does not stop exfil to an arbitrary public host unless you add an allow-list… and the DNS-off defense only kicks in for an IP-only scope. Both are opt-in. Fourth — caps truncate silently. A response past the cap is cut, not errored — so size your reads. And fifth — it's not a VPN or a proxy layer. Reaching a proxy is configuration, not something a guest negotiates… and brokered hops add a little latency a raw socket wouldn't. None of these is a bug. Each is the cost of the guest never holding a socket. You give up a little reach, and a little latency… and you get a network you can fully reason about.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can my workbook call any API? On a network profile, yes — any public host. The floor applies, so internal targets are off the table, but a normal third-party API goes through. Can it reach localhost, or my LAN? No — and not by setting, by construction. The floor denies loopback, the private ranges, the metadata address, carrier-grade NAT, and the mapped-IPv6 tricks that try to smuggle those past a naive check. How do I do HTTPS from a tiny guest with no crypto? Host TLS. The host does the handshake — you ship no TLS stack, and still speak HTTPS. Where do my API keys go? Into the engine, never the workbook. And for your own secrets the rule is sign-don't-read — the guest gets a signature, and authenticates without ever holding the key. Can I see what it tried? Yes — the audit stats and recent calls give you every attempt, with targets and reasons, plus a telemetry event for your monitoring. [chuckles] And serving — does the guest listen on a port? No. The host owns the socket. The guest only handles. And anything it fetches mid-request is still brokered — a served app can't be used as a pivot.

tracks.title: Back up to the nexus
tracks.text: So that's networking. The network isn't a switch the guest flips… it's a service the engine renders. The guest asks; the engine connects, audits, and answers — in both directions. And that single inversion is what buys HTTPS without crypto, authentication without holding the key, and a network you can revoke mid-flight. [curious] This whole page is the mechanism behind two lines on its parent lesson — no ambient network… and secrets stay in the engine. So the way back up is short. Return to the nexus — lesson two — and you'll find both of those promises stated plainly… and now you know exactly how they're kept.
